questions.question: At the opening of the chapter, why was Satī moving in and out of the room "as a swing moves this way and that"?

options.text: She was preparing decorations to welcome her father to Lord Śiva's home
Her mind was divided between the desire to see her relatives and her fear of Lord Śiva's warning
She was searching the house for her pet bird before the journey
She was performing a yogic exercise to steady her breathing

questions.explanation: "The sage Maitreya said: Lord Śiva was silent after speaking to Satī, seeing her between decisions. Satī was very much anxious to see her relatives at her father's house, but at the same time she was afraid of Lord Śiva's warning. Her mind unsettled, she moved in and out of the room as a swing moves this way and that." (Purport: "Satī's mind was divided about whether to go to her father's house or obey the orders of Lord Śiva. The struggle between the two decisions was so strong that she was pushed from one side of the room to another, and she began to move just like the pendulum of a clock.")

questions.question: According to the purport, what was the Vedic conception of the family relationship that existed between Lord Śiva and Satī when it is said he "had given her half his body"?

options.text: The husband owns the wife's body completely
The husband gives half his body to his wife, and the wife gives half of her body to her husband, so that a husband without a wife or a wife without a husband is incomplete
The wife must give her entire body to her husband while he retains his own
Half the body is given only at the time of death

questions.explanation: "According to the Vedic conception of family life, the husband gives half his body to his wife, and the wife gives half of her body to her husband. In other words, a husband without a wife or a wife without a husband is incomplete."

questions.question: The word 'apratipūruṣam' is used to describe Lord Śiva when Satī looked at him "as if she were going to blast him with her vision." What does the purport say this word means and indicate?

options.text: "One who is easily angered," indicating Śiva's temper
"One who has no equal" / "the personality who has no rival"; since Śiva is the ātmā, it indicates Satī was prepared to commit suicide
"One who lives in the crematorium," indicating his inauspicious dwelling
"One who cannot be seen," indicating Śiva's invisibility

questions.explanation: "The word apratipūruṣam, used in this verse, means 'one who has no equal.' ... In other words, since Lord Śiva is the ātmā (śiva also means ātmā), it is indicated here that Satī was prepared to commit suicide. Another meaning of the word apratipūruṣa is 'the personality who has no rival.'"

questions.question: In the purport describing Satī leaving her husband, what does the text identify as the general cause of separation and divorce between husband and wife?

options.text: Economic hardship
Interference from in-laws
Womanly behavior / womanly weakness
The husband's neglect of religious duties

questions.explanation: "Generally, separation between husband and wife is due to womanly behavior; divorce takes place due to womanly weakness. The best course for a woman is to abide by the orders of her husband. That makes family life very peaceful."

questions.question: Which of Lord Śiva's disciples are named as those who, headed the thousands of followers, quickly followed Satī when she left alone?

options.text: Nandi and Bhṛṅgi
Maṇimān and Mada
Marīci and Atri
Jagāi and Mādhāi

questions.explanation: "When they saw Satī leaving alone very rapidly, thousands of Lord Śiva's disciples, headed by Maṇimān and Mada, quickly followed her with his bull Nandi in front and accompanied by the Yakṣas."

questions.question: The word 'anucarāḥ' used to describe Lord Śiva's disciples following Satī is explained to mean what?

options.text: "Those who are afraid of their master"
"Those who ride upon bulls"
"Those who can immediately understand the purpose of their master"
"Those who chant Vedic hymns"

questions.explanation: "The word anucarāḥ is also significant, for it indicates that Lord Śiva's disciples were always ready to sacrifice anything for Lord Śiva. All of them could understand the desire of Śiva, who did not want Satī to go alone. Anucarāḥ means 'those who can immediately understand the purpose of their master.'"

questions.question: How did Lord Śiva's disciples arrange for Satī to travel to her father's house?

options.text: On foot, surrounded by an armed guard
In a golden chariot pulled by horses
Seated on the back of a bull, given her pet bird, a lotus flower, a mirror, and covered with a great canopy, in a pompous procession
Carried in a palanquin by the Yakṣas alone

questions.explanation: "The disciples of Lord Śiva arranged for Satī to be seated on the back of a bull and gave her the bird which was her pet. They bore a lotus flower, a mirror and all such paraphernalia for her enjoyment and covered her with a great canopy. Followed by a singing party with drums, conchshells and bugles, the entire procession was as pompous as a royal parade."

questions.question: Regarding the animals gathered at the sacrifice, what does the purport clarify was their real purpose?

options.text: They were meant to be killed and eaten as prasādam
They were kept as pets for the demigods
They were used to test the power of Vedic mantras — an old animal was offered in the fire and rejuvenated to test the brāhmaṇas' realization, not to be killed for meat
They were traded as payment to the priests

questions.explanation: "That these animals were meant for sacrifice does not mean that they were meant to be killed. ... to test their realization an old animal was offered in the fire and rejuvenated. That was the test of a Vedic mantra. The animals gathered were not meant to be killed and eaten. The real purpose of a sacrifice was not to replace a slaughterhouse but to test a Vedic mantra by giving an animal new life. Animals were used to test the power of Vedic mantras, not for meat."

questions.question: When Satī arrived at the sacrificial arena, who welcomed her, and why did no one else?

options.text: Her father welcomed her; the others were busy chanting
Only her mother and sisters welcomed her with tears; the others were afraid of Dakṣa
The demigods welcomed her; her family ignored her
The brāhmaṇas welcomed her; her mother was absent

questions.explanation: "When Satī, with her followers, reached the arena, because all the people assembled were afraid of Dakṣa, none of them received her well. No one welcomed her but her mother and sisters, who, with tears in their eyes and with glad faces, welcomed her and talked with her very pleasingly."

questions.question: Although her mother and sisters offered her greetings, a seat, and presents, why did Satī refuse to accept anything?

options.text: Because the gifts were impure
Because Lord Śiva had forbidden her from accepting gifts
Because her father neither talked with her nor welcomed her by asking about her welfare
Because she was fasting for the sacrifice

questions.explanation: "Although she was received by her sisters and mother, she did not reply to their words of reception, and although she was offered a seat and presents, she did not accept anything, for her father neither talked with her nor welcomed her by asking about her welfare."

questions.question: What position did Satī hold among Dakṣa's children, and how had that relationship changed?

options.text: She was the eldest and remained Dakṣa's favorite
She was the youngest child and had been his pet, but because of her association with Lord Śiva, Dakṣa forgot all his affection for her
She was a middle child whom Dakṣa never favored
She was adopted and thus never truly loved

questions.explanation: "Satī was the youngest child of Dakṣa, and she knew that she was his pet. But now, because of her association with Lord Śiva, Dakṣa forgot all his affection for his daughter, and this very much aggrieved her."

questions.question: What specific observation at the sacrifice made Satī 'greatly angry, so much so that she looked at her father as if she were going to burn him with her eyes'?

options.text: That her sisters had been given better seats than her
That there were no oblations for her husband Lord Śiva, and that Dakṣa had neither invited Śiva nor received her
That the brāhmaṇas were arguing instead of chanting
That the sacrificial animals were being mistreated

questions.explanation: "Present in the arena of sacrifice, Satī saw that there were no oblations for her husband, Lord Śiva. Next she realized that not only had her father failed to invite Lord Śiva, but when he saw Lord Śiva's exalted wife, Dakṣa did not receive her either. Thus she became greatly angry, so much so that she looked at her father as if she were going to burn him with her eyes."

questions.question: The purport states that when Viṣṇu or a Vaiṣṇava is insulted, one should be angry, and cites Lord Caitanya as an example. On whose behalf did Lord Caitanya become angry and want to kill the offenders?

options.text: When Advaita was offended by the demigods
When Nityānanda was offended by Jagāi and Mādhāi
When Haridāsa Ṭhākura was beaten in the marketplace
When His own mother was insulted

questions.explanation: "Lord Caitanya, who always preached nonviolence, meekness and humility, also became angry when Nityānanda was offended by Jagāi and Mādhāi, and He wanted to kill them. When Viṣṇu or a Vaiṣṇava is blasphemed or dishonored, one should be very angry."

questions.question: In her speech, how does Satī characterize Lord Śiva's attitude toward all living entities to prove that only Dakṣa could be envious of him?

options.text: Śiva loves only his devotees and hates the demons
Śiva is the most beloved of all living entities, has no rival, no one is very dear to him and no one is his enemy, being free from all enmity
Śiva favors the demigods above ordinary men
Śiva is indifferent and cares for no one

questions.explanation: "The blessed goddess said: Lord Śiva is the most beloved of all living entities. He has no rival. No one is very dear to him, and no one is his enemy. No one but you could be envious of such a universal being, who is free from all enmity."

questions.question: Satī addresses Dakṣa as 'dvija' (twice-born) and contrasts his fault-finding with a great soul's vision, using the analogy of what creature that seeks only honey?

options.text: A butterfly among flowers
A bee, which is always interested in the honey in the flower and does not consider the thorns and colors
A swan separating milk from water
An ant collecting only sweet grains

questions.explanation: "Just as a bee is always interested in the honey in the flower and does not consider the thorns and colors, highly qualified persons, who are uncommon, accept only the good qualities of others, not considering their bad qualities, whereas the common man can judge what are good qualities and what are bad qualities."

questions.question: In the purport to Text 12, the story of a devotee who wanted the benediction that 'whenever he touched someone on the head, that person's head would at once be separated from his trunk' is used to illustrate which name and quality of Lord Śiva?

options.text: Yogeśvara — master of yoga
Āśutoṣa — one who is satisfied very easily and offers the highest benediction, magnifying even a small good quality
Mahādeva — the greatest god
Vṛṣadhvaja — one who carries the bull banner

questions.explanation: "Lord Śiva is also called Āśutoṣa, which refers to one who is satisfied very easily and who offers to any person the highest level of benediction. For example, once a devotee of Lord Śiva wanted the benediction that whenever he touched someone on the head, that person's head would at once be separated from his trunk. Lord Śiva agreed. ... Thus Lord Śiva accepted his bad qualities as magnificently good qualities."

questions.question: Satī says the name of Lord Śiva, 'consisting of two syllables, śi and va,' does what? And what does 'śiva' mean according to the purport?

options.text: It grants wealth; śiva means 'wealthy'
It purifies one of all sinful activities; śiva means maṅgala, or auspicious
It brings victory in battle; śiva means 'conqueror'
It ensures long life; śiva means 'eternal'

questions.explanation: "Satī continued: My dear father, you are committing the greatest offense by envying Lord Śiva, whose very name, consisting of two syllables, śi and va, purifies one of all sinful activities. ... Śiva means maṅgala, or auspicious. Within the body the soul is auspicious."

questions.question: The purport uses the analogy of milk and curd (from the Brahma-saṁhitā) to explain the position of Lord Śiva relative to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. What is the point of this analogy?

options.text: Lord Śiva and Lord Viṣṇu are exactly equal, like two cups of the same milk
Lord Śiva is like curd — in one sense he is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but in another sense he is not, just as curd is milk yet we must distinguish between the two
Lord Śiva is superior to Viṣṇu, as curd is thicker than milk
Lord Śiva has no relation to Viṣṇu, as water differs from milk

questions.explanation: "Lord Śiva is described in the Brahma-saṁhitā to be like curd or yogurt. Curd is not different from milk. Since milk is transformed into curd, in one sense curd is also milk. Similarly, Lord Śiva is in one sense the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but in another sense he is not, just as curd is milk although we have to distinguish between the two."

questions.question: Satī prescribes what one should do upon hearing an irresponsible person blaspheme the master and controller of religion. What is the graded instruction she gives?

options.text: One should always forgive the blasphemer and continue chanting
If unable to punish, block one's ears and go away; but if able, one should by force cut out the blasphemer's tongue and kill the offender, and after that give up one's own life
One should report the blasphemer to the king for judgment
One should debate the blasphemer until he is convinced

questions.explanation: "Satī continued: If one hears an irresponsible person blaspheme the master and controller of religion, one should block his ears and go away if unable to punish him. But if one is able to kill, then one should by force cut out the blasphemer's tongue and kill the offender, and after that one should give up his own life."

questions.question: According to the purport of Text 17, the response to hearing blasphemy differs by social order. Why did Satī decide to give up her own body rather than kill Dakṣa?

options.text: Because she was physically unable to harm him
Because she considered herself among the vaiśyas and śūdras (with whom women are grouped), who should immediately give up their bodies upon hearing blasphemy of an exalted person
Because Lord Śiva had ordered her not to harm anyone
Because killing was forbidden inside a sacrificial arena

questions.explanation: "But as far as the vaiśyas and śūdras are concerned, they should immediately give up their bodies. Satī decided to give up her body because she thought herself to be among the śūdras and vaiśyas. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (9.32), striyo vaiśyās tathā śūdrāḥ. Women, laborers and the mercantile class are on the same level."

questions.question: Satī compares her rejection of the body received from Dakṣa to what medical analogy?

options.text: Amputating an infected limb
Vomiting — 'If someone has taken food which is poisonous, the best treatment is to vomit'
Fasting to cleanse the body
Applying medicine to a wound

questions.explanation: "Therefore I shall no longer bear this unworthy body, which has been received from you, who have blasphemed Lord Śiva. If someone has taken food which is poisonous, the best treatment is to vomit."

questions.question: According to the purport of Text 18, why did Satī — described as the representation of the external potency of the Lord, able to vanquish many universes — choose to give up her own body instead of destroying Dakṣa?

options.text: Because she feared retaliation from the demigods
To save her husband from the charge that he employed his wife to kill Dakṣa because he could not do so himself due to his inferior position
Because she had lost her powers upon entering the arena
Because the Vedas forbid a woman from killing her father

questions.explanation: "Since Satī was the representation of the external potency of the Lord, it was in her power to vanquish many universes, including many Dakṣas, but in order to save her husband from the charge that he employed his wife, Satī, to kill Dakṣa because he could not do so due to his inferior position, she decided to give up her body."

questions.question: Satī explains that when Lord Śiva addresses her by a particular name during relaxed conversation, she becomes morose and her smile disappears. What is that name and its meaning?

options.text: Bhavānī — 'wife of Bhava'
Dākṣāyaṇī — 'the daughter of King Dakṣa'
Pārvatī — 'daughter of the mountain'
Durgā — 'the invincible one'

questions.explanation: "Because of our family relationship, when Lord Śiva addresses me as Dākṣāyaṇī I at once become morose, and my jolliness and my smile at once disappear. ... The word dākṣāyaṇī means 'the daughter of King Dakṣa.' Sometimes, when there was relaxed conversation between husband and wife, Lord Śiva used to call Satī 'the daughter of King Dakṣa,' and because this very word reminded her about her family relationship with King Dakṣa, she at once became ashamed."

questions.question: After finishing her speech to Dakṣa, what did Satī do to prepare to give up her body?

options.text: She threw herself into the sacrificial fire pit
She sat down on the ground facing north, dressed in saffron/yellow garments, sanctified herself with water, closed her eyes, and absorbed herself in the mystic yoga process
She ran back toward Lord Śiva's abode
She drank poison offered at the altar

questions.explanation: "Maitreya the sage told Vidura: O annihilator of enemies, while thus speaking to her father in the arena of sacrifice, Satī sat down on the ground and faced north. Dressed in saffron garments, she sanctified herself with water and closed her eyes to absorb herself in the process of mystic yoga."

questions.question: Describe the yogic path by which Satī raised her life air before quitting her body.

options.text: From the head down to the feet
She placed the prāṇa and apāna in equilibrium near the navel, then raised the life air (mixed with intelligence) to the heart, then to the pulmonary passage, and from there to between the eyebrows
She circulated the air only within the heart
She held her breath entirely until the body stopped

questions.explanation: "First of all she sat in the required sitting posture, and then she carried the life air upwards and placed it in the position of equilibrium near the navel. Then she raised her life air, mixed with intelligence, to the heart and then gradually towards the pulmonary passage, and from there to between her eyebrows."

questions.question: By meditating on what did Satī become 'completely cleansed of all taints of sin' and quit her body in a blazing fire?

options.text: The sacrificial fire of her father
The holy lotus feet of her husband, Lord Śiva, the supreme spiritual master of all the world
The image of Lord Brahmā
The mantra of the Yajur Veda

questions.explanation: "Satī concentrated all her meditation on the holy lotus feet of her husband, Lord Śiva, who is the supreme spiritual master of all the world. Thus she became completely cleansed of all taints of sin and quit her body in a blazing fire by meditation on the fiery elements."

questions.question: According to the commentators cited in the purport of Text 27 (Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī and Śrī Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura), what happened to Satī when she 'quit her body'?

options.text: She attained a spiritual body and went to Vaikuṇṭha

She gave up her relationship with Dakṣa within her heart; being the superintendent deity of the external potency, she did not get a spiritual body but transferred to another (better) body — later taking birth as Pārvatī, daughter of the Himālayas
She merged into the Supreme and ceased to exist
She was reborn as a demigod on a higher planet

questions.explanation: "According to Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī, that Satī quit her body means that she gave up within her heart her relationship with Dakṣa. Śrī Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura also comments that since Satī is the superintendent deity of the external potency, when she quit her body she did not get a spiritual body but simply transferred from the body she had received from Dakṣa. Other commentators also say that she immediately transferred herself into the womb of Menakā, her future mother." (Also, purport to Text 26: "in her next life she would take birth as the daughter of the Himālayas, Pārvatī, and then she would again accept Lord Śiva as her husband.")

questions.question: Who is named as Satī's future mother, into whose womb she was said to have immediately transferred herself?

options.text: Aditi
Menakā
Diti
Devahūti

questions.explanation: "Other commentators also say that she immediately transferred herself into the womb of Menakā, her future mother. She gave up the body she had received from Dakṣa and immediately transferred herself to another, better body, but this does not mean that she got a spiritual body."

questions.question: What happened in the universe at the moment Satī annihilated her body in anger?

options.text: The sun went dark and the earth trembled silently
There was a tumultuous roar all over the universe, with the demigods of different planets crying out 'hā hā' in astonishment
A rain of flowers fell from the heavens
The sacrificial fire was immediately extinguished

questions.explanation: "When Satī annihilated her body in anger, there was a tumultuous roar all over the universe. Why had Satī, the wife of the most respectable demigod, Lord Śiva, quit her body in such a manner? ... There was a tumultuous roaring all over the universe in the societies of the demigods of different planets because Satī was the daughter of Dakṣa, the greatest of all kings, and the wife of Lord Śiva, the greatest of all demigods."

questions.question: The purport to Text 28 draws a lesson from Satī's dissatisfaction despite her exalted material position. What is that philosophical point (citing SB 1.2.6)?

options.text: Material opulence always guarantees happiness
Even the greatest material opulence cannot give complete satisfaction; the ātmā becomes fully satisfied only by developing devotional service to the Absolute Truth (Adhokṣaja)
Only renunciation of all activity brings peace
Satisfaction comes from family relationships alone

questions.explanation: "One cannot attain complete satisfaction even if one is situated in the greatest material opulence. ... Therefore Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.2.6) explains that one has to achieve real satisfaction (yayātmā suprasīdati), but ātmā — the body, mind and soul — all become completely satisfied only if one develops devotional service to the Absolute Truth (sa vai puṁsāṁ paro dharmo yato bhaktir adhokṣaje). Adhokṣaja means the Absolute Truth."

questions.question: When the attendants of Lord Śiva rose up with uplifted weapons to kill Dakṣa, who stopped them, and by what means?

options.text: Lord Brahmā stopped them by his personal presence
Bhṛgu Muni offered oblations into the southern side of the sacrificial fire and uttered mantric hymns from the Yajur Veda by which the destroyers of yajña could be killed
Nandi the bull blocked their path
The demigods surrounded and disarmed them

questions.explanation: "They came forward forcibly, but Bhṛgu Muni saw the danger and, offering oblations into the southern side of the sacrificial fire, immediately uttered mantric hymns from the Yajur Veda by which the destroyers of yajñic performances could be killed immediately."

questions.question: What was the outcome when Bhṛgu Muni offered oblations into the fire, and how were Satī's attendants (the Pramathas and Guhyakas) driven off?

options.text: Lord Viṣṇu appeared and pacified everyone

Many thousands of demigods named Ṛbhus became manifested, empowered by Soma the moon, and they attacked the ghosts and Guhyakas with half-burned firebrands, causing them to flee — accomplished through brahma-tejas, brahminical power
A great flood extinguished the sacrifice and scattered the crowd
Dakṣa's soldiers defeated the attendants in battle

questions.explanation: "When Bhṛgu Muni offered oblations in the fire, immediately many thousands of demigods named Ṛbhus became manifested. All of them were powerful, having achieved strength from Soma, the moon." And: "When the Ṛbhu demigods attacked the ghosts and Guhyakas with half-burned fuel from the yajña fire, all these attendants of Satī fled in different directions and disappeared. This was possible simply because of brahma-tejas, brahminical power."
